text.p: Imperial Chemical Industries Plc on Wednesday announced the $8 billion purchase of four speciality chemicals businesses from Unilever in a move which chairman Sir Ronald Hampel says will create "a new ICI for the new century".
The following is a brief history and portrait of the company, which was once seen as a barometer for British industry.

ICI is formed through the merger of four of the largest chemical companies in Britain with the aim of competing in world markets with large corporations such as DuPont in the United States and Germany's IG Farben.
Merger of Brunner, Mond & Co, Nobel Industries, British Dyestuffs Corp and United Alkali Co was agreed on the Aquitania liner on a voyage from New York to England.
It creates a group with 33,000 employees and sales in its first year of 27 million pounds. First chairman is Sir Alfred Mond, later Lord Melchett.
Over the coming decades, ICI becomes a bellwether of British industry and the London Stock Exchange.
ICI demerges its pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, specialities, seeds and biological products in June into a separate listed company, Zeneca Group Plc.
The demerger leaves ICI as a group with global businesses in industrial chemicals, paints, materials such as acrylics and polyurethanes, and explosives.
Charles Miller Smith succeeds Sir Ronald Hampel as chief executive in 1995. Hampel becomes chairman.
The group institutes a review aimed at improving productivity, broadening and deepening management and widening its product portfolio.

The strategy after the demerger of Zeneca involves shifting emphasis away from commodity chemicals which are exposed to economic cycles and towards lighter-end products such as coatings, materials and speciality chemicals with specific applications.
ICI establishes its Tioxide white pigment division as a separate structure with a view to flotation in 1997 or 1998 to raise some 1.5 billion pounds.

May 7: ICI announces the $8 billion purchase of four speciality chemicals businesses from Unilever and the sale through a global offering of its 62.4 percent stake in ICI Australia Ltd, worth around one billion pounds.

Acquisition of the Unilever businesses will add more than 15,000 employees worldwide, including 2,500 in Britain. The units had operating profits of 357 million pounds in 1996 on revenues of 2.93 billion pounds.

ICI currently has some 63,200 employees with manufacturing operations at about 200 sites in more than 30 countries. ICI profit before tax and exceptional items fell in 1996 to 603 million pounds on sales of 10.52 billion from 951 million pounds in 1995.
